body: I'm generally not terribly interested in the details here; I just filed the issues because I was looking at some code in Gecko that dealt with referrer policies and there were obvious problems with that code, so I looked at the spec and the spec was problematic too. Oh, and there are serious problems with the wpt test coverage, leading to minor attempts like https://github.com/w3c/web-platform-tests/pull/2851 to fix that. The total black hole there does not help me care about this topic, obviously. ;) One other thing for the future: these pull requests for the HTML spec are _much_ easier to review when I have an actual generated spec to look at instead of having to reverse-engineer it from the diff. Anyway, on the substance... What Gecko does, I believe, is store the referrer policy in the thing that gets aliased when origin needs to alias, but does snapshot it at document creation time, copying it from that aliased thing. Note that this applies to more than just nested browsing contexts; for example I'm pretty sure we copy the referrer policy when doing `window.open()` (no url). I have no idea what other browsers do, and there is no test coverage for this afaict. Looks to me like this spec proposal does do that, at first glance. I don't know that "local URL" is the right thing to be using. That includes "filesystem"; do we really want to inherit referrer policies for those? The bit about "Otherwise (e.g., if the navigation was to a URL with a local scheme)" doesn't make sense to me either. If I navigate to a blob: is there not a `response`? In what actual situations is there no `response`? If I have a document with referrer policy A which creates a subframe, then a document with referrer policy B navigates that subframe to a blob:, is the referrer policy of the result A or B? It should be B. I think this spec proposal makes it A. One last thing is what should happen with history traversal. This is currently pretty broken anyway because https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#history-traversal step 1 uses "source browsing context", but the relevant scenario is this one: 1. A document D1 with referrer policy P1 loads URL U1 in a subframe. 2. The subframe is then navigated to a different URL U2. 3. The referrer policy of D1 is changed to P2. 4. The user clicks the back button. Which referrer policy is used when determining the referrer for the navigation to U1? Is it P1 or P2? Gecko uses P1; we actually capture the referrer and referrer policy used for the load in the history entry that results from loading U1, so we can replay the same exact fetch later. Again, I have no idea what other browsers do and there is no test coverage.

Unfortunately I don't understand that workers section at all either. @jeisinger do you know what's going on there by any chance (https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-referrer-policy/#referrer-policy-delivery-implicit-workers)?

My best guess is that the intention was for workers to have the default policy (`no-referrer-when-downgrade`), and if there is a Referrer-Policy header in the worker's main script response, then that referrer policy should be applied for the worker. Does that sound at all reasonable?

> My best guess is that the intention was for workers to have the default policy (no-referrer-when-downgrade), and if there is a Referrer-Policy header in the worker's main script response, then that referrer policy should be applied for the worker. Does that sound at all reasonable?

This sounds somewhat reasonable, but let me propose an alternative semantics:
- Fetching the worker itself uses the fetching client's referrer policy. (I.e., if fetching from a document, the one set by the header/meta tag for the document; if fetching from a worker, the one set in the next bullet point.)
- When the worker is fetched, check any Referrer-Policy header, and store it on the worker, so that future fetches from within that worker (importScripts, XHR, fetch, `import`, ...) all use that referrer policy by default.

I think we agree on bullet point two but IMO using the fetching client's referrer policy makes more sense than always using no-referrer-when-downgrade.

Ah, I was only thinking about fetches that the worker made. Using the
fetching client's policy when fetching the worker itself sgtm.

If there is no referrer policy header from fetching the worker, I think it
should probably just use the default for any fetches that the worker makes?

IIRC that matches how csp works: the fetching client's csp is applied when
fetching the worker itself, then the csp served with the worker script is
applied to fetches that the worker makes (and no csp if none was served
with the worker script)

The paragraph is supposed to define what happens if no referrer-policy header is in the response. In your two bullet points, it's then undefined which referrer policy to use, and the paragraph says that fetches from such an worker should use the default policy then.

Sorry, it was implicit in my paragraphs, I agree. To be more clear: the worker referrer policy would stay at the  default of "", which in the "set request's referrer" algorithm, gets treated the same as no-referrer-when-downgrade, assuming there is no more specific override (e.g. via the fetch() API)

I'll work on updating to reflect those bullet points and pong for another review when that's done. Not sure about the navigation stuff still, though. Maybe I'll try to see if we can copy CSP more closely or something...

OK, it turns out I had already implemented those bullet points, so we should be good.

I looked at the navigation stuff more, and I think @bzbarsky is right that the local scheme division doesn't make sense. I think this is derived from [CSP's similar algorithm](https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-csp/#initialize-document-csp), but CSP says:

> Note: We do all this to ensure that a page cannot bypass its policy by embedding a frame or popping up a new window containing content it controls (blob: resources, or document.write()).

I don't believe this concern applies here; we don't need to "ratchet" the referrer policy to stay always as strict as the document's referrer policy. We can always override it by using `fetch` with a custom `referrerPolicy` option.

So I switched it to just always parsing the Referrer-Policy header, instead of only doing that for non-local schemes. Note that this doesn't quite mesh with my understanding of @bzbarsky's position:

>  If I have a document with referrer policy A which creates a subframe, then a document with referrer policy B navigates that subframe to a blob:, is the referrer policy of the result A or B? It should be B. I think this spec proposal makes it A.

I don't think we want to use the referrer policy of the document that initiated navigation as the referrer policy of the newly navigated-to document. Instead, I think we want to reset the referrer policy every navigation, based on the Referrer-Policy header (and falling back to "", which gives "no-referrer-if-downgrade" behavior). Thus, this is similar to the HTTPS state of the document.

---

So, this is ready for review, and IMO merge. Would love some sign-offs if people have the time.

The https state of the result loading a "blob:" is the https state of the thing that started the load.  I'm just saying referrer policy should work that way too...

Note that this is pretty specific to blob: and a few other schemes.  Obviously if an http:// URI is loaded, its referrer policy should come from headers.

> The https state of the result loading a "blob:" is the https state of the thing that started the load. I'm just saying referrer policy should work that way too...

Hmm, is the spec currently wrong on that too? :( It currently says, in the navigate algorithm's "initialising a new Document object",

> Set the Document's HTTPS state to the HTTPS state of the resource used to generate the document.
I guess maybe the complexity is hidden in the probably-underspecified process by which this "resource" is created...

>    Set the Document's HTTPS state to the HTTPS state of the resource used to generate the document.

Right, but the fetch spec propagates HTTPS state to blob responses.  See https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#basic-fetch the "blob:" part step 6.  Wish I could link to things more directly in that spec...
Oh, thanks. It looks like we should do the same thing for referrer policy then.
Yes!   That's what I was trying to say in https://github.com/w3c/webappsec-referrer-policy/issues/32 but not clearly enough.
See also https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/issues/270 about where blob URLs should grab HTTPS state from. The current thinking is that it should be stored on `Blob` objects directly.
Sure, but that leaves https state for about:blank anyway...

LGTM with that caveat.

At some point we should really refactor the document creation algorithms so that it's very clear what state gets copied across.
